findings.issue: The general “Mismatch” row overgeneralizes that the solvent has “its own, stronger forces.” A force mismatch does not necessarily mean solvent–solvent attractions are stronger than solute–solute attractions, and this wording also makes solubility seem controlled only by the solvent.
findings.evidence: The source says that mismatched IMFs do not let solvent particles surround and stabilize solute particles as effectively; stronger water–water hydrogen bonding is specific to the iodine/water worked example. As standard chemistry, a polar or hydrogen-bonding solute can have stronger self-interactions than a nonpolar solvent’s London dispersion forces. The general point is that the new solute–solvent attractions do not adequately compensate for the solute–solute and/or solvent–solvent interactions disrupted, not that the solvent’s forces are necessarily stronger.
